messages.subject: Need for speed
parts:
Hi nimble devs! 
I am currently working a spatial analysis that requires a fair amount of raster calculations populating rasterStacks (using the raster package with well specified vectorized operations). Currently, I have an R function that does these calculations in R and have been using it within a nimble model with the nimleRcall() function. This appears to be working. For the broader analysis that I am doing, however, I am considering how to get this process to run as fast as possible. I have found that nimble functions even after compilation are slow when they require the creation of large matrixes/arrays within them.... especially when passing those rasters back to the nimble mcmc object. I plan to only return values that I need for the likelihood in this function, but I will still need to do an extensive amount of raster calculations. Would you recommend doing this in a nimble function or would it be faster to write this in a C++ function and then access it using nimbleExternalCall()? If I'm taking the time to implement this, I am wondering what the fastest method may be?
I greatly appreciate any advice y'all may have regarding this. 
Thanks!
--Alison

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Need for speed
parts:
Hi Alison,

Sounds interesting, good to hear from you, and thanks for posting.

Do you need the large objects actually in the model?  I can't quite follow, but it sounds like maybe not.  If not, you could leave them in R and let the nimbleRcall use them there.  Does that make sense?

You could also do that in C++, as follows.  The nimbleExternalCall interfacing is still rudimentary and can only call a simple C++ function.  If you have some C++ experience, you could have a class in C++ (or even simply global objects) that can hold the data you need (populated from R such as via Rcpp or .C and .Call) and do the work there.  You'd just need the simple C++ function called from nimbleExternalCall to invoke the work you need done.

One small trick is to use init=FALSE when you create large matrices/arrays in nimbleFunctions.  That's only a good idea if you will be explicitly populating every element and not relying on default values (0 or otherwise).  It can make a noticeable but not game-changing difference in efficiency.

I'm probably not getting the problem clearly, but HTH and feel free to follow up.

Perry
